chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Alawi from al-Amriki from Safwan from Ali ibn Matar from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Indeed, two men disputed over a beast of burden before Ali (peace be upon him). Each claimed it had given birth to it at his place, on his milking stand. Each presented evidence, equal in number. So he cast lots between them with two arrows, marking each arrow with a sign for each of them. Then he said: "O God, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the seven earths and Lord of the Great Throne, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Whichever of them is the owner of the beast and has more right to it, I ask You to cast lots and bring forth his name." So the name of one of them came out, and he ruled in his favor. And it was also the case when the two disputants argued over a female slave, one claiming he bought her and the other claiming he had her give birth, that when they both presented evidence, he ruled in favor of the one at whose place she had given birth.'
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali resolve a dispute when both parties presented equal evidence of ownership?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) employs the method of *qur'a* (casting lots) as a form of divine arbitration (*hukm bi-qismat Allah*) when two parties present equally valid evidence (*bayyinah*) for ownership of a beast. This case illustrates the Shia juristic principle that when evidentiary weight is equal, the decision may rest on a divinely guided random selection, accompanied by a specific supplication invoking Allah as the Knower of the Unseen. The text further establishes a comparative legal precedent for female slaves, where the party who gave birth to her holds superior claim, highlighting the nuanced application of evidence in early Islamic jurisprudence.
